strengths: The paper targets an important and underexplored problem: assessing visualization quality requires more than conventional chart question answering or generic image-aesthetics evaluation.
VISJUDGE-BENCH is reasonably large and diverse, containing 3,090 real-world examples spanning single charts, multi-view visualizations, dashboards, and 32 reported subtypes.

The six-dimensional rubric is useful for diagnostic evaluation, and the paper compares several strong proprietary and open multimodal models using MAE, MSE, correlation, distributional analysis, and qualitative cases.
VISJUDGE substantially improves over its Qwen2.5-VL-7B base model and achieves the best reported test-set results, suggesting that domain-specific supervision is valuable.
The manuscript is generally well organized and includes extensive appendices describing prompts, annotation interfaces, filtering, and training hyperparameters.
weaknesses: The validity of the central Data Fidelity dimension is questionable because the benchmark supplies only rendered images, not the underlying data or chart specifications. Annotators and models can identify visible scale or encoding problems, but generally cannot determine whether a chart faithfully represents its source data. The paper repeatedly overstates this as data accuracy or truthfulness.

The claimed expert ground truth is insufficiently validated. Initial labels come from broadly screened crowd workers rather than demonstrated visualization experts, while the qualifications and adjudication behavior of the three experts are vague. No inter-annotator agreement, expert-expert agreement, reliability by dimension, confidence intervals, or comparison against independent expert labels is reported. Moreover, 58% of scores were altered through expert calibration, making the final-label construction especially consequential.

The main model comparison is not controlled: VISJUDGE is directly trained on labels from the benchmark, whereas all other models are evaluated zero-shot. There are no supervised-regression, calibration, prompt-tuning, SFT, or simple mean/type-conditioned baselines, and no ablation establishing that GRPO, rationales, adaptive questions, or the proposed framework cause the gains.

The random stratified image split risks substantial source, template, publisher, and near-duplicate leakage across train and test. Perceptual-hash deduplication before splitting does not address semantically duplicated charts or dashboards from the same website/template. There is no source-disjoint split or evaluation on an independently collected external dataset.

Several analyses and claims conflict with the reported numbers. The paper states that models perform relatively well on Fidelity and struggle most on Aesthetics, yet Table 3 generally shows larger fidelity errors than aesthetic errors. Pooled correlation of 0.681 also drops to 0.375-0.577 within visualization categories, so part of the headline result may arise from between-category score differences rather than strong within-category ranking.

The experimental reporting lacks uncertainty and statistical testing despite stochastic three-run inference. It is therefore unclear whether several baseline differences are meaningful. The scaling-law claim is also too strong for a handful of points from one dataset and one training configuration; a logarithmic correlation fit of R²=0.628 is not a well-established scaling law.

The stated 70%/10%/20% split is arithmetically inconsistent with the reported counts: 2,163/279/648 correspond to approximately 70%/9%/21%. The scaling experiment further uses up to 2,442 samples, exactly the combined training and validation count, without explaining the role of validation data.

Reproducibility and release readiness are incomplete: the abstract ends with an empty availability statement, model/API versioning and inference details are incomplete, and the manuscript does not provide auditable image provenance or licensing information beyond asserting compliance. These issues are particularly important for a benchmark built from crawled web images.

strengths: The paper targets an important and underexplored problem: assessing visualization quality beyond conventional chart question answering.
The benchmark is reasonably large, containing 3,090 visualizations spanning single charts, multi-view compositions, dashboards, and 32 reported subtypes.
The proposed six-dimensional rubric is more informative than a single aesthetic score, and the evaluation includes several strong commercial and open multimodal models.
The authors provide useful analyses of score bias, visualization complexity, training-set size, and representative failure cases.
weaknesses: The central fidelity construct is not validly measured. The benchmark contains chart images but no underlying source data, so annotators and models generally cannot determine whether the displayed values faithfully represent the data. They can only inspect visible conventions such as baselines, scales, and label consistency. This substantially weakens claims about evaluating data accuracy or truthfulness.

The claimed expert ground truth is insufficiently validated. Initial labels come from broadly screened crowdworkers rather than demonstrated visualization experts; the qualifications of the three adjudicating experts are not reported; and no inter-annotator reliability statistic, expert-expert agreement, or uncertainty analysis is provided. This is particularly concerning because 58% of samples were reportedly recalibrated by experts.

Item-specific questions and rubrics are generated using GPT-4o from the same images. The paper does not quantify generation errors, validate these questions independently, or clearly isolate how generated descriptions affect human and model judgments. Different adaptive rubrics may also compromise score comparability across examples.

The experimental design does not establish generalization. Splits are random and stratified only by visualization type, with no grouping by website, template, topic, or source. Perceptual-hash filtering before splitting does not rule out related templates or semantically near-duplicate web images across train and test sets. There is also no evaluation on an independently collected dataset.

The model comparison conflates domain training with modeling quality. VISJUDGE is explicitly optimized on benchmark labels, while the commercial baselines are used zero-shot. Missing controls include supervised fine-tuning, simpler regression or calibration baselines, alternative preference-learning objectives, and ablations of GRPO, LoRA, the accuracy reward, and adaptive prompts.

Reported gains lack confidence intervals, significance tests, variation across training seeds, and human-label ceilings. Consequently, differences such as MAE 0.551 versus 0.442 cannot be assessed relative to annotation noise.

The claimed scaling laws are not supported by a sufficiently rigorous experiment: curves are fitted to a small number of training sizes using one-epoch runs, apparently without repeated sampling or uncertainty estimates. High fitted R² values alone do not establish a scaling law.

Several interpretations contradict the table. The paper says models perform relatively well on Fidelity and struggle most with Aesthetics, although baseline fidelity MAEs are generally larger than aesthetic MAEs. VISJUDGE also remains weak on some dimensions, including only 0.385 correlation for color harmony and substantially reduced performance on dashboards.

The generated rationales are not evaluated for correctness, faithfulness, or usefulness, even though producing justifications is presented as part of the task. The format reward only checks whether required JSON fields exist.

Reproducibility and data governance are inadequate for a benchmark contribution. The manuscript leaves the benchmark URL blank, does not provide inference versions/dates and sufficient API details, and gives no clear release or licensing plan. Crawling images through Bing also raises unresolved copyright, attribution, and redistribution concerns.

Overall, the benchmark direction is promising, but weaknesses in construct validity, annotation reliability, leakage control, baselines, statistical analysis, and release details prevent the work from being competitive at a top-tier AI venue in its current form.

strengths: The paper targets an important and underexplored problem: assessing visualization quality requires more than generic image aesthetics or chart question answering.
VISJUDGE-BENCH is substantial in scale and breadth, with 3,090 real-world examples spanning single charts, multi-view visualizations, dashboards, and 32 subtypes.
The fidelity–expressiveness–aesthetics framework is intuitive, grounded in visualization literature, and operationalized into six useful diagnostic dimensions.

The annotation pipeline includes multiple annotators, attention checks, disagreement detection, and expert adjudication; the extensive appendix provides prompts, rubrics, interfaces, and training details.
The evaluation covers a broad selection of proprietary and open MLLMs, reports complementary error and correlation metrics, and includes breakdowns by dimension and visualization complexity.
VISJUDGE produces large improvements over its Qwen2.5-VL-7B base model and all evaluated zero-shot models, suggesting that domain-specific supervision is valuable.
The manuscript is generally clear and visually polished, with helpful distribution analyses and qualitative examples.
weaknesses: The central fidelity construct is not fully valid from screenshots alone. Without the underlying data or chart specification, annotators generally cannot determine whether plotted values faithfully represent the source data; they can only detect visible or internal inconsistencies. The paper nevertheless makes broad claims about data accuracy.

Annotation reliability is insufficiently quantified. Although the paper says the design enables inter-annotator agreement analysis, it reports no ICC, Krippendorff's alpha, pairwise agreement, confidence intervals, or agreement before and after adjudication. This is a major omission for a benchmark whose ground truth is subjective.

The claimed expert ground truth is unclear: initial labels come from broadly screened crowd workers rather than demonstrated visualization experts, while the qualifications of the three adjudicators and the exact adjudication protocol are only vaguely described. Moreover, 58% of scores were changed during expert calibration, making validation of this stage especially important.

The adaptive questions and textual chart descriptions are generated by GPT-4o and shown to annotators, but their factual accuracy and potential anchoring effects are not evaluated. Hallucinated descriptions could systematically affect both labels and model comparisons.

VISJUDGE is trained directly on the benchmark labels while the strongest comparisons are zero-shot general-purpose models. This demonstrates in-domain fitting but not generalization. There is no external dataset, source-domain split, cross-template test, or human study showing that the model transfers to unseen visualization distributions.

Reported improvements lack uncertainty estimates, significance tests, multiple training seeds, or sensitivity analyses. Calling the small-sample curve a predictable scaling law based on one run per scale and simple fitted trends is overstated.

Several methodological statements are inconsistent or questionable: the paper states that all inference uses vLLM even though proprietary GPT, Claude, and Gemini models cannot be run through vLLM; it calls the evaluation seven models while listing seven baselines plus VISJUDGE; and the 2,442-sample scaling experiment exceeds the stated 2,163-example training split without clearly explaining use of the validation set.

Some analysis contradicts Table 3. The text says models perform relatively well on Fidelity and struggle most on Aesthetics, yet the displayed MAE values are generally worse for Fidelity than for the aesthetic dimensions. The abstract also highlights correlation improvement over GPT-5 even though GPT-4o is the strongest correlation baseline.

The web-crawled images raise reproducibility, provenance, and licensing concerns. The ethics statement asserts compliance with copyright and usage terms, but the paper does not explain source tracking, licenses, takedown procedures, or whether redistribution of all images is permitted. The promised benchmark URL is also absent from the manuscript.
The benchmark distribution is highly uneven within subtypes—some chart types have only one to three examples—so claims of coverage across all 32 types are stronger than the evidence supports.

strengths: Addresses an important, under-benchmarked problem: holistic assessment of visualization fidelity, expressiveness, and aesthetics.
Introduces a broad corpus of 3,090 real-world examples spanning 32 chart types, including single charts, multi-view visualizations, and dashboards.
Provides detailed evaluation criteria, annotation procedures, prompts, case studies, and quality-control documentation.
Evaluates numerous proprietary and open-source MLLMs and demonstrates consistent fine-tuning gains across four model architectures.
Includes downstream generation and recommendation experiments that attempt to establish practical utility beyond in-benchmark prediction.
weaknesses: The central data-fidelity construct cannot be fully assessed from screenshots without underlying data. The benchmark detects visible inconsistencies rather than whether a chart faithfully represents its source data, weakening claims of comprehensive fidelity evaluation.

Ground-truth reliability is not established rigorously enough for subjective, expertise-dependent judgments. Most initial annotators are crowd workers, only three ratings are collected per item, the expert pool contains only three people, and expert-expert agreement, ICC/Krippendorff's alpha, and label uncertainty are not reported.

The random stratified split does not convincingly prevent leakage. Web search can return cropped, resized, restyled, or template-related images; global pHash deduplication alone does not establish source-, website-, template-, or domain-disjoint evaluation.

Results lack confidence intervals, paired significance tests, training-seed variance, and sensitivity analysis for prompts or decoding. Consequently, the robustness of reported model rankings and improvements is unclear.

The baseline protocol is insufficiently reproducible: proprietary model versions and access dates are not clearly pinned, and the statement that all inference uses vLLM is incompatible with ordinary evaluation of proprietary APIs.

The proposed learning method has limited novelty, combining standard LoRA and GRPO with direct score-matching rewards. No ablations compare against supervised fine-tuning, simple calibration, or isolate GRPO, rationales, adaptive questions, and reward components.

Downstream evidence is not fully convincing. MatPlotAgent outputs are evaluated automatically by GPT-4o rather than humans or task-grounded metrics, while sample sizes and statistical uncertainty are omitted; HAIChart improvements are modest and likewise lack significance analysis.

Several interpretations are overstated or inconsistent with the evidence: aesthetics is described as the most difficult area despite lower reported MAE than fidelity/readability, matching the human mean is called near-perfect distributional alignment despite moderate correlations, and limited downstream tests are used to claim deployment readiness.

The planned release of web-scraped images raises unresolved copyright and provenance concerns. The ethics statement asserts compliance but does not document licenses, source attribution, redistribution rights, or takedown procedures; geographic concentration of annotators also limits the generality of aesthetic judgments.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful and relatively underexplored problem: assessing visualization quality with multimodal models rather than only testing chart question answering or generation.
VISJUDGE-BENCH has substantial breadth, with 3,090 visualizations spanning single charts, multi-view compositions, dashboards, 32 subtypes, six assessment dimensions, and varied quality levels.
The empirical study includes numerous proprietary and open-source models, dimension-level metrics, score-distribution analysis, qualitative examples, and fine-tuning across four model families.
The authors document the collection and annotation pipeline extensively and make a meaningful effort toward quality control.
weaknesses: The benchmark has a fundamental construct-validity problem: source data are unavailable, so “data fidelity” is inferred only from rendered images. The annotations cannot verify whether displayed values are correct and instead conflate fidelity with visible design conventions, missing labels, and readability. This materially weakens the central claim of comprehensive visualization-quality assessment.

The claimed expert ground truth is insufficiently validated. Most labels originate from general crowdsourcing workers, while three vaguely characterized experts adjudicate scores using algorithmically proposed transformations. The paper reports neither expert qualifications in adequate detail nor expert-expert agreement. Its crowd-crowd MAE is computed against an average containing the evaluated annotator, making it optimistically biased; standard reliability measures such as ICC or Krippendorff's alpha are absent.

The rubric itself is debatable. It treats novelty and uniqueness as intrinsic quality, potentially penalizing conventional but effective statistical graphics. “Insight discovery” also depends heavily on task and audience context that web images do not provide. GPT-4o-generated, image-specific questions may introduce hallucinations or inconsistent rubrics, but their quality is not independently audited.

The main evaluation uses a random image-level split from web search results. Perceptual-hash filtering does not rule out related templates, alternate exports, or charts from the same source crossing splits. There is no source-grouped split or independent human-labeled external test set, so memorization and source leakage remain plausible.

The reported gains lack uncertainty estimates, significance tests, or repeated-training-seed analysis. Selecting the best of four fine-tuned backbones on the same benchmark further favors the proposed method. Matching the human score mean is presented as “human-like behavior,” although marginal distribution alignment does not establish per-example agreement.

The downstream evidence is weak. MatPlotAgent outputs are judged solely by GPT-4o, with no human evaluation, sample sizes, confidence intervals, or significance tests. HAIChart gains are modest and likewise lack uncertainty. These experiments do not justify claims of production readiness or broad out-of-distribution generalization.

The “scaling law” claim is unsupported by a small set of points from one dataset and one training run; fitting logarithmic or exponential curves and reporting R-squared values is not evidence of a scaling law. The maximum stated training size of 2,442 also conflicts with the earlier 2,163-sample training split unless validation data were reused, which is not explained.

Reproducibility is incomplete and internally inconsistent. The manuscript says all inference used vLLM on local A6000 GPUs even though proprietary models cannot be run that way, omits precise API/model snapshots and several decoding details, and promises future release rather than providing an accessible artifact. Web-image licensing and redistribution are asserted to be compliant without concrete provenance or license analysis.

strengths: VISJUDGE-BENCH addresses an important and underexplored problem: assessing visualization fidelity, expressiveness, and aesthetics rather than only chart question answering or text-to-visualization correctness.
The dataset is substantial, containing 3,090 real-world examples spanning single charts, multi-view visualizations, dashboards, and 32 subtypes, with six fine-grained rating dimensions.
The annotation effort is extensive: three crowd ratings per example, validation checks, expert review of all examples, disagreement-resolution procedures, and analyses across annotator backgrounds.

The empirical study covers a strong collection of closed- and open-source MLLMs, multiple model architectures, per-dimension and per-visualization-type results, score-bias analysis, and qualitative failure cases.

Fine-tuning consistently improves all four tested backbones. The best model substantially improves MAE and correlation over both its base model and strong proprietary baselines, providing credible evidence that domain-specific supervision is useful.

The downstream generation and recommendation experiments broaden the paper beyond an in-benchmark fine-tuning result, while the planned release of annotations, quality-control records, and model weights would be a useful community resource.
weaknesses: The validity and independence of the ground truth are insufficiently established. Expert scores are treated as a gold standard, but the experts reviewed crowd scores and algorithmically proposed resolutions rather than clearly performing an independent annotation. Approximately 73% of examples retained all original crowd ratings, and no inter-expert agreement or blinded expert-versus-crowd comparison is reported. Consequently, the crowd–expert MAE is partly circular and does not strongly validate label reliability.

The benchmark calls one dimension “data fidelity,” although source data are unavailable. It can therefore detect only visually apparent encoding problems, not whether plotted values faithfully represent the underlying data. Some central claims about accuracy and truthfulness are stronger than this evidence permits.

GPT-4o-generated chart descriptions, questions, and item-specific rubrics are shown to annotators, but their factual accuracy and neutrality are not systematically audited. Hallucinated metadata or leading criteria could influence both human labels and models, creating model-induced benchmark bias.

The random stratified split is not source- or template-disjoint. Perceptual-hash deduplication with a strict threshold does not rule out near-duplicate charts, shared dashboard templates, or variants from the same webpage crossing splits, so memorization and leakage remain plausible.

Statistical reporting is incomplete: there are no confidence intervals, significance tests, seed-level variability, or uncertainty estimates for the reported model differences. Several relevant test subtypes have very small sample counts.

The model is trained to emit rationales, but evaluation measures only numeric scores. There is no assessment of whether explanations correctly identify visualization flaws, despite qualitative claims about diagnostic feedback.

The MatPlotAgent study is evaluated solely by GPT-4o rather than independent humans, making the claimed downstream quality gains vulnerable to judge bias. Sample sizes, uncertainty, and significance are also omitted for both downstream applications.

The framework embeds debatable value judgments—for example, treating novelty and uniqueness as universally desirable design quality—and gives limited attention to task context, accessibility, cultural variation, or different user populations. The annotator pool is overwhelmingly US-based.

Claims of “predictable scaling laws,” strong out-of-distribution generalization, and production readiness are overstated relative to the small number of training scales and limited downstream evaluations. Overall, the resource is promising, but these central validation gaps place it slightly below the top-tier acceptance threshold.
